ripple_effect.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, and China retaliated with its own tariffs, including on U.S. agricultural exports.
historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to some of the highest levels in a century; Canada, France, and other major trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs within months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: World trade volumes fell by roughly two-thirds over the following four years; widely cited by economists as having deepened and prolonged the Great Depression globally, not just in the U.S. — the clearest historical example that a major tariff escalation's damage isn't confined to the two countries directly involved.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan
historical_precedents.what_happened: After Japan detained a Chinese trawler captain following a collision near the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands, China informally slowed rare earth mineral shipments to Japan without declaring a formal ban.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). ripple_effect.name: GLP-1 obesity/diabetes drugs reshaping healthcare cost and pharma markets

historical_precedents.event: Novo Nordisk's Ozempic/Wegovy-driven rise to Europe's most valuable company, then competitive erosion
historical_precedents.what_happened: Demand for Novo Nordisk's GLP-1 drugs Ozempic (approved for diabetes, widely used off-label for weight loss) and Wegovy (approved for obesity) grew so rapidly that weight-loss drugs made up 55% of the company's 2023 revenue and its first-half 2023 profit rose 45% year-over-year; by March 2024 the company reached a $604 billion market capitalization, the 12th most valuable company in the world, and by April 2024 its roughly $570 billion market cap exceeded the size of Denmark's entire economy, with its roughly $2.3 billion Danish corporate tax bill alone driving nearly all of Denmark's measured economic growth that year.
historical_precedents.market_impact: US list prices for these drugs ran far above prices charged elsewhere (Ozempic around $969/month in the US versus $155 in Canada and $59 in Germany; Wegovy around $1,349/month in the US versus $140 in Germany and $92 in the UK), fueling a US health-insurance and employer-benefit-design debate over covering the drugs at scale; by July 2025, rising competitor pressure had pushed Novo down to the fifth most valuable drugmaker by market cap, prompting a CEO change effective August 7, 2025.

possibility_chains: A single drug class becoming a large share of a national economy's growth, as with Novo Nordisk and Denmark, has historically made that country's headline GDP figures unusually sensitive to one company's product cycle.

Insurers and employers facing a costly new high-demand drug class have historically responded first with coverage restrictions (prior authorization, BMI thresholds) before broadening access as production scales and price competition emerges.

A manufacturer's inability to keep pace with demand for a breakout drug has historically triggered shortages, compounding-pharmacy workarounds, and counterfeit-product risk in the gap before supply catches up.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Novo Nordisk's Ozempic/Wegovy-driven rise to Europe's most valuable company, then competitive erosion (2022–2025): US list prices for these drugs ran far above prices charged elsewhere (Ozempic around $969/month in the US versus $155 in Canada and $59 in Germany; Wegovy around $1,349/month in the US versus $140 in Germany and $92 in the UK), fueling a US health-insurance and employer-benefit-design debate over covering the drugs at scale; by July 2025, rising competitor pressure had pushed Novo down to the fifth most valuable drugmaker by market cap, prompting a CEO change effective August 7, 2025. A single drug class becoming a large share of a national economy's growth, as with Novo Nordisk and Denmark, has historically made that country's headline GDP figures unusually sensitive to one company's product cycle.

linked_playbooks.name: Pharmaceutical patent cliff and blockbuster drug revenue loss
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Lipitor (atorvastatin) patent expiration (1996–2012 (US patent expired November 30, 2011)): Generic prices stayed relatively elevated during that initial exclusivity window, then fell sharply once additional manufacturers entered in May 2012, pushing a month's supply down toward standard generic pricing of $10 or less — illustrating the two-stage price collapse (moderate initial generic discount, then a much steeper one once multiple generic makers compete) that characterizes a typical pharmaceutical patent-cliff event. A cluster of blockbuster drugs (defined in the industry as over $1 billion in annual sales) losing patent protection in the same multi-year window has historically pushed large pharmaceutical companies toward M&A, portfolio diversification, and 'evergreening' strategies (new formulations or delivery mechanisms) to offset the revenue drop.

linked_playbooks.name: Aging population driving healthcare system cost and capacity pressure
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Japan's healthcare spending rise under a super-aged population (2008–2018): Japan introduced a dedicated long-term care insurance system (Kaigo-Hoken), funded partly by a roughly 2% income contribution from residents over 40 and administered by municipal governments, specifically to fund elderly care costs separately from general health insurance as the aging-driven cost pressure became structural rather than cyclical; by 2016 the system was allocating tens of billions of dollars annually toward long-term care expenditures. A country crossing the 'super-aged society' threshold (21%+ population 65+) has historically required either new dedicated funding mechanisms, as with Japan's long-term-care insurance, or rising general healthcare spending as a share of GDP, or both.

ripple_effect.name: Oil-exporter sanctions collapse

historical_precedents.what_happened: The US Treasury imposed sanctions on Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA, blocking it from receiving payment for petroleum exports to the US, freezing roughly $7 billion in US-based assets, and barring US firms from exporting the diluents Venezuela's heavy crude needs in order to be exported, as part of a push to pressure President Nicolás Maduro to leave office.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The Trump administration's National Security Advisor estimated the sanctions would cost Venezuela's economy over $11 billion in 2019 alone; some buyers, including firms from India, Spain, and Russia, continued purchasing Venezuelan crude or supplying diluents through alternative arrangements, showing that sanctions on a major exporter's oil sector reduce but do not eliminate its ability to sell, especially when buyers outside the sanctioning coalition are willing to continue trade.

possibility_chains: Sanctions targeting a major oil exporter's state company have historically forced that country to sell at a discount to buyers outside the sanctioning coalition, reducing but not eliminating export revenue.

An oil-dependent economy cut off from its normal export markets and financing has historically seen its currency, government budget, and imports of basic goods deteriorate sharply, compounding pre-existing economic weakness.

Global oil markets have historically absorbed the loss of a sanctioned mid-sized exporter's output with a relatively modest price effect, since other producers have generally had spare capacity to partly offset the loss — unlike a shock to the largest exporters.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: US sanctions on PDVSA (January 2019): The Trump administration's National Security Advisor estimated the sanctions would cost Venezuela's economy over $11 billion in 2019 alone; some buyers, including firms from India, Spain, and Russia, continued purchasing Venezuelan crude or supplying diluents through alternative arrangements, showing that sanctions on a major exporter's oil sector reduce but do not eliminate its ability to sell, especially when buyers outside the sanctioning coalition are willing to continue trade. Sanctions targeting a major oil exporter's state company have historically forced that country to sell at a discount to buyers outside the sanctioning coalition, reducing but not eliminating export revenue.

linked_playbooks.name: Sanctions imposed on a major economy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: International sanctions on Iran over its nuclear program (2010s): Iranian oil exports fell sharply, though global oil prices were also affected by supply from other producers filling the gap; Iran's own currency and economy experienced significant strain during the most restrictive sanctions periods. Sanctions targeting a major energy or commodity exporter have historically tightened global supply of that commodity, which has often (though not always, depending on how much other producers can offset the loss) pushed prices higher.

linked_playbooks.name: US shale boom and oil price crash
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Shale-driven oil glut and price collapse (2014-2016): Crude oil prices, which had been above $100 a barrel through mid-2014, fell below $30 a barrel by January 2016; the collapse triggered internal economic crises in oil-dependent OPEC members including Venezuela, Algeria, Libya, and Nigeria, with Venezuela's crisis — its exports were about 96% oil-dependent — becoming one of the worst peacetime economic collapses on record. A prolonged period of low oil prices has historically forced high-cost producers, including US shale operators, to cut spending and idle rigs, though shale's shorter well-cycle times have made US output recover faster than in prior boom-bust cycles.

linked_playbooks.name: G7 price cap on sanctioned oil exports
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: G7/EU/Australia price cap on Russian seaborne crude oil (December 2022 onward): Russian crude traded well below the cap in the following weeks — reported as low as about $45 a barrel at Baltic ports — and Russia's weekly oil export duty revenue reportedly fell by around 60%; Russia responded by building a large 'shadow fleet' of older tankers (estimated at over 1,000 vessels by late 2023) operating outside Western insurance and shipping services to sell oil above the cap. A price cap enforced through control of shipping and insurance services (rather than a direct import ban) has historically been partially evaded by the sanctioned country building an alternative fleet and insurance arrangement outside the sanctioning coalition's reach.

linked_playbooks.name: Sharp currency devaluation / currency crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Turkish lira crisis (2018): The lira lost roughly 30–40% of its value against the U.S. dollar over the year, sharply raising the cost of imports and foreign-currency debt for Turkish businesses. A sharp currency devaluation has historically made imported goods, including fuel and food, significantly more expensive for consumers and businesses in the affected country.

ripple_effect.name: Extreme heatwave drives mass mortality, crop losses, and power-grid strain

historical_precedents.what_happened: An extreme, prolonged heatwave across Europe in July-August 2003 -- the hottest European summer since at least 1540 -- killed an estimated 72,000 people, including roughly 20,000 in Italy, 14,800-19,000 in France, nearly 13,000 in Spain, 9,500 in Germany, 2,000 in the UK, and about 1,950 in Portugal, where the temperature reached a record 47.3 degC (117.1 degF) at Amareleja on August 1, 2003.
historical_precedents.market_impact: European economic losses were estimated at about 0.5% of European GDP overall, with more than 1% GDP loss in the hardest-hit regions. Wheat harvests fell short by 20% in France, 13% in Italy, and 12% in the UK, cutting total EU production by about 10 million tonnes (10%). On the power grid, thermal and nuclear plants in several countries faced restrictions on discharging cooling water into overheated rivers: Germany saw reduced hydroelectric output and rising electricity prices, Italy imposed rolling blackouts as consumption surged, and France's own power exports dropped by 800 megawatts as domestic demand competed with generation constraints.

possibility_chains: Extreme heatwaves have historically caused mass excess mortality concentrated among elderly and vulnerable populations, with death tolls that were substantially undercounted in real time and only became clear in retrospective statistical analysis weeks or months later.

Sustained extreme heat has historically constrained thermal and nuclear power generation simultaneously with a surge in cooling-driven electricity demand, creating grid stress at exactly the moment supply is most limited.

A single severe heatwave affecting a major agricultural region has historically cut cereal harvests broadly across several neighboring countries at once, since the same weather system typically spans national borders.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: 2003 European heatwave (July-August 2003): European economic losses were estimated at about 0.5% of European GDP overall, with more than 1% GDP loss in the hardest-hit regions. Wheat harvests fell short by 20% in France, 13% in Italy, and 12% in the UK, cutting total EU production by about 10 million tonnes (10%). On the power grid, thermal and nuclear plants in several countries faced restrictions on discharging cooling water into overheated rivers: Germany saw reduced hydroelectric output and rising electricity prices, Italy imposed rolling blackouts as consumption surged, and France's own power exports dropped by 800 megawatts as domestic demand competed with generation constraints. Extreme heatwaves have historically caused mass excess mortality concentrated among elderly and vulnerable populations, with death tolls that were substantially undercounted in real time and only became clear in retrospective statistical analysis weeks or months later.

linked_playbooks.name: Major drought or heatwave affecting crop yields
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: East Africa drought and Somali famine (2010–2011): An estimated 260,000 people died in Somalia alone, roughly half of them children under five, and millions were displaced across the region — a reminder that crop-yield shocks in the world's poorest, import-dependent regions have historically produced humanitarian catastrophe rather than the price-inflation effects seen in wealthier grain-exporting economies. A severe drought or heatwave affecting a major agricultural exporting region has historically reduced crop yields and raised global prices for that crop, with the size of the effect depending on how much of global supply the affected region represents.

linked_playbooks.name: Cascading power grid blackout
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Northeast blackout of 2003 (14-16 August 2003): Roughly 55 million people lost power, including 14.3 million in the New York City area, 8.3 million in the Toronto area, and 6.4 million in metropolitan Detroit; the blackout prompted the eventual creation of mandatory, enforceable electric reliability standards in the US and Canada, since none existed at the time of the failure. A localized equipment or software fault on a highly interconnected grid has historically cascaded far beyond its origin point, since protective systems designed to isolate faults can also propagate them if operators lose situational awareness in time.

linked_playbooks.name: Nuclear power shutdown or phase-out
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Germany's nuclear phase-out (2011-2023): Between 2002 and 2022 Germany's fossil-fuel energy use rose about 7% even as nuclear was phased out, with natural gas use increasing the most; a 2020 academic study estimated the shift from nuclear toward coal-fired generation cost Germany roughly €3-8 billion a year in social costs, mostly from air-pollution-linked deaths. A country that rapidly removes a large share of its baseload nuclear generation has historically had to replace it with a combination of fossil-fuel imports and renewable buildout, with the fossil-fuel share dominating in the near term given how long new generation capacity takes to build.

The tribunal ruled on 12 July 2016 that China's historic-rights claim had no lawful basis under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that none of the disputed Spratly Islands features qualified as islands generating their own exclusive economic zone.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China rejected the ruling as null and void and continued its island-building and patrol activities in the disputed waters. The ruling did not resolve the underlying dispute, and multiple claimant states (Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, Taiwan) continue to assert overlapping claims to parts of the same waters, through which a large share of global seaborne trade transits.

ripple_effect.name: Desert locust plague devastates crops across a region

historical_precedents.event: 2019–2022 desert locust upsurge across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and South Asia
historical_precedents.what_happened: Unusual cyclone activity in 2018 (Cyclones Mekunu and Luban) created breeding conditions in the Arabian desert that let locust populations multiply roughly 8,000-fold across three generations. The resulting swarms spread into Kenya (its worst outbreak in over 70 years), Ethiopia (worst in 25 years), Somalia, Uganda, South Sudan, Eritrea, and Djibouti, and later into Yemen, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, India, Iran, and Nepal, before the surge was officially declared over in February 2022.
historical_precedents.market_impact: By April 2020, roughly 2.25 million hectares were affected; the World Bank estimated potential agricultural damage across Africa could reach $9 billion, with long-term response costs exceeding $1 billion. The UN reported that 20.2 million people across the affected region faced severe acute food insecurity as swarms destroyed crops and pasture.

possibility_chains: A major locust upsurge has historically required sustained, cross-border coordination among affected governments and international agencies, since swarms migrate across national boundaries following weather patterns rather than respecting them.
Unusual cyclone or rainfall patterns in normally arid breeding grounds have historically been an early-warning signal for locust population booms months before crop damage becomes visible.
Regions already facing conflict or weak state capacity have historically struggled most to mount an effective locust response, compounding food-insecurity effects beyond the direct crop losses.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: 2019–2022 desert locust upsurge across East Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and South Asia (June 2019 – February 2022): By April 2020, roughly 2.25 million hectares were affected; the World Bank estimated potential agricultural damage across Africa could reach $9 billion, with long-term response costs exceeding $1 billion. The UN reported that 20.2 million people across the affected region faced severe acute food insecurity as swarms destroyed crops and pasture. A major locust upsurge has historically required sustained, cross-border coordination among affected governments and international agencies, since swarms migrate across national boundaries following weather patterns rather than respecting them.

linked_playbooks.name: Major drought or heatwave affecting crop yields
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: East Africa drought and Somali famine (2010–2011): An estimated 260,000 people died in Somalia alone, roughly half of them children under five, and millions were displaced across the region — a reminder that crop-yield shocks in the world's poorest, import-dependent regions have historically produced humanitarian catastrophe rather than the price-inflation effects seen in wealthier grain-exporting economies. A severe drought or heatwave affecting a major agricultural exporting region has historically reduced crop yields and raised global prices for that crop, with the size of the effect depending on how much of global supply the affected region represents.

ripple_effect.name: Fuel subsidy removal triggers public unrest

historical_precedents.what_happened: The government removed Nigeria's longstanding petrol subsidy on January 1, 2012, roughly doubling pump prices from 65 to at least 141 naira per litre; nationwide strikes and protests followed for nearly two weeks (January 2–14) across Lagos, Abuja, Kano, and other cities, with trade unions announcing an indefinite strike from January 9.
historical_precedents.market_impact: About 16 people were killed in clashes between protesters and police, and the government partially walked back the increase before the standoff ended.

historical_precedents.event: Ecuador's Decree 883 fuel subsidy removal and reversal
historical_precedents.what_happened: President Lenín Moreno eliminated 40-year-old fuel subsidies on October 1, 2019 as part of an IMF-linked austerity package addressing $64 billion in debt, roughly doubling diesel prices and raising petrol prices about 30%; indigenous groups (CONAIE), transport workers, and students staged nationwide protests from October 3–14.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The unrest left 8 dead, over 1,300 injured, and nearly 1,200 detained; President Moreno reversed the policy by signing Decree 894 on October 14, 2019, restoring subsidies to previous levels after a televised agreement with indigenous leaders.

possibility_chains: Sudden, large fuel subsidy removals (rather than gradual phase-outs) have historically triggered the fastest and largest public backlash, since the price change is immediate and highly visible to every driver and transport-dependent business at once.

Fuel subsidy cuts tied explicitly to IMF or multilateral lender conditions have historically been politically riskier for a government to sustain than domestically-initiated cuts, since opponents can frame the policy as externally imposed.

Governments facing sustained fuel-subsidy protests have historically had to choose between accepting significant political and fiscal cost from unrest or reversing the policy and returning to the fiscal drain the subsidy represented — full reversal has been a common outcome even after violent confrontations.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Ecuador's Decree 883 fuel subsidy removal and reversal (October 2019): The unrest left 8 dead, over 1,300 injured, and nearly 1,200 detained; President Moreno reversed the policy by signing Decree 894 on October 14, 2019, restoring subsidies to previous levels after a televised agreement with indigenous leaders. Sudden, large fuel subsidy removals (rather than gradual phase-outs) have historically triggered the fastest and largest public backlash, since the price change is immediate and highly visible to every driver and transport-dependent business at once.

linked_playbooks.name: IMF bailout or rescue program for a sovereign
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's IMF Extended Fund Facility after its 2022 default (2022–2024): The program aimed to raise Sri Lanka's tax-to-GDP ratio from 8.1% in 2021 to 15% by 2025, but the accompanying austerity coincided with unemployment rising from 5.7% to 8.3% between 2022 and 2023. IMF rescue programs have historically come attached to austerity conditions (tax increases, spending cuts, structural reforms) that have often produced short-term economic pain — higher unemployment, reduced public services — even where they are intended to restore longer-term stability.

linked_playbooks.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

ripple_effect.name: Peacekeeping or foreign military mission withdrawal

historical_precedents.event: French and UN force withdrawal from Mali
historical_precedents.what_happened: France and its European partners announced in February 2022 a full withdrawal of Operation Barkhane forces from Mali within six months, amid tensions with Mali's ruling military junta over its use of Wagner Group mercenaries. In 2023, at the junta's request, the UN peacekeeping mission MINUSMA withdrew and handed over its twelve military bases to Malian authorities.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The handover of former peacekeeping bases heightened tensions between Mali's government and Tuareg-led separatist groups over control of bases in the Kidal region, contributing to renewed armed conflict in northern Mali in 2023-2024.

possibility_chains: The withdrawal of peacekeeping or foreign stabilization forces from a conflict-affected country has historically created a security vacuum that armed groups already present have sought to fill, particularly around handed-over military infrastructure.

Governments that request the departure of international forces have historically done so amid friction over sovereignty or alternative security partnerships, a dynamic that has often coincided with a shift in the departing country's broader foreign alignment.
Areas that lose international peacekeeping presence have historically seen protection and humanitarian access for civilians decline, a pattern documented across multiple UN mission drawdowns.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: French and UN force withdrawal from Mali (February 2022 – 2023): The handover of former peacekeeping bases heightened tensions between Mali's government and Tuareg-led separatist groups over control of bases in the Kidal region, contributing to renewed armed conflict in northern Mali in 2023-2024. The withdrawal of peacekeeping or foreign stabilization forces from a conflict-affected country has historically created a security vacuum that armed groups already present have sought to fill, particularly around handed-over military infrastructure.

linked_playbooks.name: Civil war spilling over into neighboring countries
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: ISIL's capture of Mosul, Iraq, following gains made during Syria's civil war (June 2014): The rapid collapse of Iraqi forces and the territorial gains that followed prompted the Iraqi government to request international assistance and led to the formation of a U.S.-led coalition against ISIL later that year; the episode illustrated how a civil war in one country can directly enable an insurgency's rapid territorial expansion into a neighboring state. An armed group that gains territory, weapons, or resources in one country's civil war has historically used that strength to expand operations across the border into a neighboring, weaker state.

linked_playbooks.name: Armed conflict driving a large-scale refugee crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Syrian refugee crisis (2011–2016): A World Bank report found the refugee influx cost Jordan more than $2.5 billion a year, equivalent to about 6% of its GDP, and Jordan's public debt rose to about 95% of GDP by 2016. By contrast, a UNDP/ILO study estimated Syrian refugees contributed around $800 million to Egypt's economy over a comparable period, illustrating that the fiscal impact of hosting refugees has varied significantly by host country's labor market and refugee employment patterns. A large, sudden refugee outflow from a conflict has historically placed the greatest fiscal and infrastructure strain on the conflict's immediate neighbors, who typically host far larger refugee populations, proportionally and often absolutely, than more distant destination countries.

ripple_effect.name: Major tariff escalation / trade war

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. imposed tariffs on hundreds of billions of dollars of Chinese goods, and China retaliated with its own tariffs, including on U.S. agricultural exports.
historical_precedents.market_impact: U.S. soybean exports to China fell sharply, and the U.S. government paid out tens of billions of dollars in subsidies to farmers hurt by the retaliation; global manufacturers reported higher input costs and supply-chain uncertainty through the period.

historical_precedents.what_happened: The U.S. raised tariffs on over 20,000 imported goods to some of the highest levels in a century; Canada, France, and other major trading partners retaliated with their own tariffs within months.
historical_precedents.market_impact: World trade volumes fell by roughly two-thirds over the following four years; widely cited by economists as having deepened and prolonged the Great Depression globally, not just in the U.S. — the clearest historical example that a major tariff escalation's damage isn't confined to the two countries directly involved.

historical_precedents.event: China's rare earth export restrictions on Japan
historical_precedents.what_happened: After Japan detained a Chinese trawler captain following a collision near the disputed Senkaku/Diaoyu Islands, China informally slowed rare earth mineral shipments to Japan without declaring a formal ban.
historical_precedents.market_impact: China's rare earth exports fell roughly 77% year-on-year by September 2011, and global prices spiked several-fold (cerium oxide rose from around $4.70/kg in April 2010 to around $36/kg that October). The U.S. filed a WTO case in 2012; the WTO ruled against China in 2014, and China dropped its export quotas in 2015 — but the episode had already pushed Japan and other importers to diversify sourcing and boost recycling.

possibility_chains: New tariffs have historically raised the cost of the affected imported goods, at least part of which has often been passed on to consumers or absorbed as lower profit margins by importers.

historical_precedents.market_impact: This level of dependence has historically made Tajikistan's economy highly sensitive to labor-market and currency conditions in Russia: a slowdown in Russian labor demand, tighter migration policy, or a weaker ruble has fed directly through into reduced household income and foreign-currency inflows at home.

historical_precedents.event: Remittances exceed a quarter of GDP in multiple Asian and Latin American economies
historical_precedents.what_happened: World Bank-era estimates for 2023 put remittances at roughly 35% of GDP in Nepal, about 19.3% in Guatemala, and about 17.8% in Uzbekistan, while the Philippines — one of the largest recipients in absolute dollar terms — received remittances equal to roughly 9.2% of GDP that year.
historical_precedents.market_impact: In each of these economies, remittances functioned as a larger and comparatively more stable source of foreign currency than either foreign direct investment or official development aid, cushioning consumption during domestic downturns but also transmitting external labor-market shocks from destination countries.

historical_precedents.event: Global remittance flows grow more than tenfold over two decades
historical_precedents.what_happened: Global remittance flows rose from about $72.3 billion in 2001 to about $549 billion in 2019 and about $780 billion sent to roughly 800 million people in 2021.
historical_precedents.market_impact: The sustained growth in remittance flows made diaspora labor migration one of the largest channels of cross-border financial support to developing economies, growing faster over this period than global foreign direct investment flows to the same country group.

possibility_chains: A sharp slowdown in a major migrant-labor destination economy has historically reduced remittance inflows to dependent source countries with a lag of a few months, since migrants have tended to draw down savings or reduce discretionary transfers before returning home outright.

Because remittances are typically spent on household consumption rather than invested in productive capacity, remittance-dependent economies have historically shown resilient consumer spending during global downturns but have also shown limited translation of remittance inflows into broad-based domestic investment or export diversification.

A currency devaluation in a remittance-dependent recipient country has historically increased the local-currency value of a fixed dollar remittance, temporarily boosting recipient households' purchasing power even as the devaluation raises the cost of imported goods economy-wide.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Global remittance flows grow more than tenfold over two decades (2001–2021): The sustained growth in remittance flows made diaspora labor migration one of the largest channels of cross-border financial support to developing economies, growing faster over this period than global foreign direct investment flows to the same country group. A sharp slowdown in a major migrant-labor destination economy has historically reduced remittance inflows to dependent source countries with a lag of a few months, since migrants have tended to draw down savings or reduce discretionary transfers before returning home outright.

linked_playbooks.name: Gulf states' kafala guest-worker system
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Qatar reforms labor rules ahead of hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup (2018–2021): Despite the announced reforms, international labor-rights organizations, including Human Rights Watch, documented continued gaps between stated policy and workplace practice, illustrating how migrant-labor-dependent Gulf construction and hospitality sectors faced sustained international scrutiny tied to labor conditions through a major global sporting event. Economies with a very high share of the workforce composed of tied-visa migrant labor have historically been able to expand or contract large construction and infrastructure projects (such as World Cup stadium building) faster than economies reliant primarily on domestic labor, since labor supply can be scaled up through recruitment rather than constrained by local workforce size.

linked_playbooks.name: Venezuela's mass emigration and regional economic strain
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sudden border-region strain in Brazil (Late 2016): The influx strained local health, housing, and social services in one of Brazil's poorest and least populous states, becoming an early flashpoint in the broader regional migration crisis. A sudden, sustained mass emigration from an economically collapsing country has historically concentrated disproportionately in geographically or culturally proximate neighboring countries first, before spreading to more distant destinations as migration networks and legal pathways develop.

linked_playbooks.name: Sharp currency devaluation / currency crisis
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Turkish lira crisis (2018): The lira lost roughly 30–40% of its value against the U.S. dollar over the year, sharply raising the cost of imports and foreign-currency debt for Turkish businesses. A sharp currency devaluation has historically made imported goods, including fuel and food, significantly more expensive for consumers and businesses in the affected country.

ripple_effect.name: Low-cost carriers disrupt legacy airline pricing after deregulation

historical_precedents.event: Ryanair adopts the low-cost carrier model as EU aviation deregulation takes effect
historical_precedents.what_happened: Ryanair restructured itself into a low-cost carrier starting in 1990, after its founders studied Southwest Airlines' model in the United States; the airline standardized on an all-Boeing 737 fleet and cut its cheapest return fare from £99 to £59. When Ryanair had launched its Dublin-London Luton route in 1987 under partial EEC air-travel deregulation, it priced return fares at £99 — roughly half the prevailing legacy-carrier rate — prompting Aer Lingus and British Airways to cut their own fares to £95 and £94.99 in response. The EU's Single Aviation Market, established in 1992, and further deregulation in April 1997 removed remaining cabotage restrictions and enabled Ryanair's rapid pan-European expansion, with annual passengers growing from about 745,000 in 1990 to 66.5 million by 2010.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Ryanair's model was subsequently adopted by other low-cost carriers including easyJet, WestJet, and AirAsia, restructuring competitive pricing across the European aviation market over the following decades.

historical_precedents.event: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers
historical_precedents.what_happened: Following the 1978 US Airline Deregulation Act, low-cost carriers such as Southwest Airlines expanded point-to-point service that competed directly with legacy hub-and-spoke carriers on price.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones.

possibility_chains: A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

Sustained low-cost-carrier competition following deregulation has historically compressed average industry fares over a period of years to decades, with the effect concentrated on the routes most exposed to new low-cost entrants.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: US Airline Deregulation Act and the growth of low-cost, point-to-point carriers (1978–1994): Average US fares per passenger mile fell about 9% between 1979 and 1994, and inflation-adjusted fares fell roughly 30% between 1976 and 1990; a New York-Los Angeles round trip that would have cost an inflation-adjusted $1,442 in 1974 could be purchased for around $268 by 2010, though these savings accrued more to higher-traffic, longer-distance routes than to shorter ones. A low-cost carrier entering a new route or market has historically forced incumbent legacy carriers to cut their own fares on that route in direct response, rather than cede the market entirely.

linked_playbooks.name: 2008–2015 US airline merger wave consolidates the industry into four major carriers
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: American Airlines merges with US Airways (February–December 2013): The merger created what became, by some measurements, the largest airline in the world by passengers carried and scheduled passenger-kilometers flown, completing a consolidation wave that also included United Airlines' 2010 merger with Continental — leaving the US domestic market dominated by four major carriers (American, Delta, United, and Southwest). A period of sustained high fuel costs or post-recession financial stress has historically accelerated airline merger activity, as weaker carriers sought scale and stronger balance sheets through consolidation rather than standalone survival.

linked_playbooks.name: Thomas Cook collapse triggers UK's largest peacetime repatriation
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Collapse of Thomas Cook Group (September 2019): The UK Civil Aviation Authority launched 'Operation Matterhorn,' chartering roughly 40 aircraft from other carriers including easyJet, Virgin Atlantic, and Malaysia Airlines to repatriate stranded travelers — an operation the CAA said overtook the 2017 collapse of Monarch Airlines as the UK's largest peacetime repatriation. About 21,000 Thomas Cook employees worldwide lost their jobs, including 9,000 in the UK; the company had reported a £1.5 billion loss for the first half of 2019, including £1.1 billion in goodwill write-downs. A major tour operator or airline's sudden collapse has historically stranded large numbers of travelers simultaneously, forcing government-coordinated emergency repatriation using capacity chartered from competing airlines.

ripple_effect.name: US territory / sub-sovereign debt restructuring crisis

historical_precedents.event: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring
historical_precedents.what_happened: Puerto Rico's bonds were downgraded to junk status in February 2014, and Governor García Padilla declared the roughly $74 billion in bond debt (plus $49 billion in unfunded pension liabilities) 'not payable' on June 28, 2015; after Puerto Rico missed a $422 million payment on May 1, 2016, Congress passed PROMESA, which President Obama signed June 30, 2016, creating a federal oversight board with authority over the territory's budget and debt restructuring.
historical_precedents.market_impact: Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022.

possibility_chains: A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

Heavy institutional exposure to a single distressed municipal issuer (in this case, via tax-exempt bond funds that concentrated Puerto Rico debt for its tax advantages) has historically transmitted a regional fiscal crisis into national investment portfolios far from the issuer itself.

Debt-crisis austerity measures layered on top of a shrinking population and tax base have historically been self-reinforcing, since tax increases and service cuts have tended to accelerate the outward migration that shrank the tax base in the first place.
ripple_effect.why_it_matters: Puerto Rico's government-debt crisis and PROMESA restructuring (2014–2022): Puerto Rico's poverty rate reached roughly 45% by mid-2017, unemployment hit 12.4% in December 2016, and its sales tax rose to 11% alongside teacher retirement-age increases (47 to 62) and 10% pension cuts under the oversight board's austerity plan; nearly 70% of US municipal bond funds held Puerto Rico exposure, and its general obligation bonds fell to roughly 32 cents on the dollar after Hurricane Maria in 2017 before the territory exited bankruptcy in March 2022. A US territory's debt crisis has historically been resolved through federal oversight mechanisms different from either a state (which cannot file Chapter 9 the way cities can) or an independent country (which cannot access IMF facilities), creating restructuring rules unique to the territory's ambiguous status.

linked_playbooks.name: Major municipal or county bankruptcy
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Jefferson County, Alabama bankruptcy (November 2011 – December 2013): The county cut its government workforce by more than 700 employees by May 2012, and the bankruptcy court wrote off more than $1.4 billion of the debt before the county emerged from bankruptcy in December 2013. A municipal bankruptcy driven by a shrinking tax base and rising legacy retiree costs has historically forced a choice between deep pension cuts and finding outside funding (such as philanthropic support) to soften them, since the two options are not fiscally separable.

linked_playbooks.name: Government austerity program (spending cuts and tax rises)
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Canada's 1995 federal budget under Finance Minister Paul Martin (1995): By shrinking the federal transfer, the reform shifted fiscal pressure onto provincial governments, which had to make their own cuts to health and social assistance spending to absorb the reduced federal contribution. Government austerity programs that cut public sector employment have historically taken years to fully play out in local labor markets, as affected workers and the local businesses that served them adjust gradually rather than all at once.

linked_playbooks.name: Sovereign government debt default
linked_playbooks.why_it_matters: Sri Lanka's first sovereign default (April 2022): The default followed foreign reserves falling to just $1.9 billion by March 2022, insufficient to cover the country's import and debt-service needs, and led into an IMF rescue program. A sovereign default has historically triggered a sharp loss of access to international capital markets for the defaulting government, often for years, forcing reliance on domestic financing or multilateral lenders in the interim.
